title: Research or Quality Work? Belmont Principles and the IRB
summary: Trace US research-ethics rules from the Tuskegee syphilis study to the Belmont principles, then use the Common Rule definition of research to decide which laboratory projects need IRB review, and how exempt, expedited and full reviews differ.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 14 Hits 1–5 and 10 and Traps 1 and 6 (first lesson for Ch. 14). Regulatory points from the Common Rule (45 CFR 46.102, 46.104, 46.107, 46.109, 46.110) and HIPAA (45 CFR 160.103), eCFR version 2026-10-01; Belmont principles and applications from Nagai 2022; Tuskegee history from Tobin 2022. The Belmont Report itself and OHRP guidance pages could not be fetched (HTTP 403) and were not read. Who makes exemption determinations is set by institutional policy, not the regulation text (register flag rv-exempt-determiner). Not taught as fact: the HIPAA Omnibus Rule date, case-report rule, clinical-trial phase sizes, Moore v. UCLA, kickbacks, record-retention periods, discarded-serum retention, anonymous vs deidentified data, research billing.

objectives: Name the three Belmont principles and their applications.
Apply the Common Rule definition of research to laboratory activities such as method verification and QC.
Distinguish exempt, expedited and convened IRB review and state the IRB membership rules.

scenes.title: Research, or just quality work?
scenes.altText: Invented scenario with three projects from one US laboratory: (1) a verification study of a new troponin method before it goes live; (2) the same QC data, which the supervisor now plans to publish; (3) a study pulling identifiable patient records from several hospitals to test whether a biomarker predicts outcomes. Question token: “Which needs an IRB?”

cues.text: One laboratory has three projects. First, it verifies a new troponin method before using it on patients.
Second, the supervisor wants to publish those same verification data. Third, a team will pull identifiable records from several hospitals to test whether a biomarker predicts outcomes.
Which of these needs review by an institutional review board?

scenes.title: Why the rules exist
scenes.altText: Timeline card: in the US Public Health Service study of untreated syphilis at Tuskegee (1932–1972), investigators withheld effective therapy from hundreds of African American men for 40 years, even after penicillin became the treatment of choice; congressional hearings after its exposure led to the National Research Act, institutional review boards and informed-consent protections. Belmont card: the Belmont Report (submitted 1978, released 1979) rests on three principles — RESPECT FOR PERSONS, BENEFICENCE, JUSTICE — with three applications: informed consent, assessment of risks and benefits, and selection of subjects.

cues.text: In the US Public Health Service syphilis study at Tuskegee, from 1932 to 1972, investigators withheld effective treatment from hundreds of African American men, even after penicillin became the standard therapy.
Its exposure led to congressional hearings and the National Research Act, which brought institutional review boards and informed-consent protections.
The Belmont Report then set out three principles: respect for persons, beneficence, and justice.
Each has an application: informed consent, weighing risks against benefits, and fair selection of subjects.

scenes.title: What counts as research, and who reviews it
scenes.altText: Definition card (US Common Rule, 45 CFR 46.102(l)): RESEARCH is “a systematic investigation … designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge.” Routine method verification, QC and quality improvement aimed at the lab’s own performance are not designed for generalizable knowledge. IRB card (46.107): at least 5 members; at least one whose primary concerns are scientific and one nonscientific; at least one not otherwise affiliated with the institution. Review-type card: EXEMPT categories (46.104); EXPEDITED review by the chair or designated experienced members, who may not disapprove (46.110); CONVENED (full) IRB review with continuing review at least once a year (46.109(e)); continuing review is generally not required for expedited-eligible research unless the IRB decides otherwise (46.109(f)).

cues.text: Under the US Common Rule, research is a systematic investigation designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge. Routine method verification, QC and quality improvement for the lab’s own use are not designed for that.
An institutional review board has at least five members, including a scientist, a non-scientist, and someone not affiliated with the institution.
Some research falls into exempt categories. Minimal-risk studies on the expedited list can be reviewed by the chair or designated members, who may approve but may not disapprove.

Other studies go to the convened board, with continuing review at least once a year. Under the revised Common Rule, expedited studies usually need no continuing review unless the board decides otherwise.

scenes.title: Sort the three projects
scenes.altText: Decision cards. (1) Method verification before go-live: quality work for the lab’s own testing, not designed for generalizable knowledge → not research under 46.102(l). (2) Publishing the same data: what makes an activity research is its design and purpose, not the plan to publish (the reviewer cites OHRP policy on this; the app did not read that guidance). Check the institution’s policy. (3) Systematic outcome study using identifiable records from several hospitals → research; it needs IRB review (or an IRB/institutional exemption determination) BEFORE data collection. Privacy card: under HIPAA, protected health information excludes information about a person who has been dead for more than 50 years (45 CFR 160.103) — so records of patients who died less than 50 years ago are still protected.

cues.text: Sort the projects. Verifying a method before go-live is quality work for the lab itself. It is not designed for generalizable knowledge, so it is not research.
Publishing those data does not by itself turn them into research. Design and purpose decide. Still, follow your institution’s policy.
The multi-hospital outcome study is a systematic investigation for generalizable knowledge. It is research and needs IRB review before any data are pulled.
And patient records stay protected under HIPAA until fifty years after death.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Planning to publish makes QC data research” (✓ research is defined by systematic design for generalizable knowledge, not by publication); “Expedited studies need annual continuing review” (✓ under the revised Common Rule, generally not, unless the IRB decides otherwise; convened-board studies are reviewed at least yearly); “An expedited reviewer can reject a protocol” (✓ expedited reviewers may approve or require changes but may not disapprove; disapproval needs the convened IRB).

cues.text: Trap one: planning to publish makes QC data research. No: research is defined by a systematic design aimed at generalizable knowledge.
Trap two: expedited studies need yearly continuing review. Under the revised Common Rule they generally do not, unless the board decides otherwise.
Trap three: an expedited reviewer can reject a protocol. No: expedited reviewers may not disapprove research; only the convened board can.

scenes.title: Ask, weigh, share fairly
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Belmont asks three questions: Did you ASK? (respect for persons → informed consent) Did you WEIGH? (beneficence → risks vs benefits) Did you SHARE FAIRLY? (justice → fair selection of subjects). Research is the PLAN to learn something for everyone, not the plan to publish.” Tokens: ask · weigh · share fairly. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Belmont asks three questions. Did you ask? That is consent. Did you weigh? That is risks against benefits. Did you share fairly? That is fair subject selection. And research is a plan to learn for everyone, not a plan to publish.

Where it breaks: these are US rules; other countries, including the Philippines, have their own research-ethics systems; institutions decide who makes exemption calls; and FDA-regulated studies follow additional rules.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Belmont: respect for persons → consent · beneficence → risk/benefit · justice → fair selection”, “Research = systematic, for generalizable knowledge (46.102(l)) · IRB ≥5 members · expedited can’t disapprove · PHI to 50 yr after death”.

cues.text: The Belmont principles of respect for persons, beneficence and justice become informed consent, risk–benefit assessment and fair subject selection, and under the US Common Rule an activity is research, needing IRB review before it starts, when it is a systematic investigation designed for generalizable knowledge.

props.label: Respect → consent · beneficence → risk/benefit · justice → selection
Research = systematic, generalizable · IRB ≥5 · PHI to 50 yr

explanation.what: Plain language: studies on people must ask permission, weigh harm against benefit, and choose participants fairly. A project counts as research when it is planned to produce knowledge useful beyond your own lab; then an ethics board must review it before it starts. Routine checks of your own tests are not research. Scientific terms: Belmont Report, respect for persons, beneficence, justice, informed consent, Common Rule, research (systematic investigation, generalizable knowledge), institutional review board (IRB), exempt, expedited and convened review, continuing review, protected health information (PHI).
explanation.why: The rules were built after abuses such as the Tuskegee study, in which effective treatment was withheld for decades without honest consent. Defining research by its design keeps quality work flexible while protecting people whose data are used to create general knowledge.
explanation.measure: Research: systematic investigation designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge (46.102(l)). IRB: ≥5 members, ≥1 scientific, ≥1 nonscientific, ≥1 unaffiliated (46.107). Expedited review by chair/designated reviewers who may not disapprove (46.110(b)). Convened-IRB research: continuing review at least yearly (46.109(e)); expedited-eligible research: generally no continuing review unless the IRB decides otherwise (46.109(f)). PHI excludes information on persons dead > 50 years (160.103).
explanation.differs: Quality work vs research; exempt vs expedited vs convened review; expedited reviewer (approve/modify) vs convened IRB (can disapprove).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name or apply a Belmont principle, decide whether a lab activity is research, identify IRB membership requirements, or recall the HIPAA 50-year rule and the revised continuing-review rule.

mnemonic.text: Belmont asks three questions: Did you ASK? (respect for persons → informed consent) Did you WEIGH? (beneficence → risks vs benefits) Did you SHARE FAIRLY? (justice → fair selection of subjects). Research is the PLAN to learn something for everyone, not the plan to publish.

questions.stem: Which Belmont principle is applied mainly through informed consent?

options.rationale: Correct. Respect for persons is applied through informed consent.
Incorrect. Beneficence is applied through assessment of risks and benefits.
Incorrect. Justice is applied through fair selection of subjects.
Incorrect. Not one of the three Belmont principles; avoiding harm falls under beneficence.

questions.stem: A US laboratory verifies a new method before patient use and later decides to publish the data. Under the Common Rule definition, what determines whether this is research?

options.text: Whether it is a systematic investigation designed to contribute to generalizable knowledge
options.rationale: Correct. 45 CFR 46.102(l) defines research by design and purpose.

options.text: Whether the results will be published
options.rationale: Incorrect. Publication alone does not define research.

options.text: Whether more than 100 samples are tested
options.rationale: Incorrect. Sample size is not part of the definition.

options.text: Whether the lab director signs the report

questions.stem: Which IRB composition meets the minimum requirements of 45 CFR 46.107?

options.text: Five members, including a scientist, a non-scientist and one member not affiliated with the institution
options.rationale: Correct. At least five members with these three roles represented.

options.text: Three scientists from the same department
options.rationale: Incorrect. Too few members, and no non-scientist or unaffiliated member.

options.text: Five physicians, all employed by the hospital
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lacks a non-scientist and an unaffiliated member.

options.text: The principal investigator and the lab director
options.rationale: Incorrect. Investigators cannot form the IRB reviewing their own work, and two is too few.
